newsitem.title: UK: Discounting in ex-UK air cargo mkt at year's start.
newsitem.headline: Discounting in ex-UK air cargo mkt at year's start.

text.p: Average ex-UK air cargo rates have changed little in the past two weeks but this ignores some substantial but selective discounts offered by British Air, a Reuters survey shows.
Sterling's strength against most nearly all currencies will help keep a lid on ex-UK sterling denominated cargo rates, forwarders and airline sources said.
But those operating to dollar markets where sterling has made smaller movements said the fluctuations have been inside a manageable range.

The currency impact has been most noticeable on the London to South Africa route but this reflects delayed reaction to the earlier decline of the rand in foreign exchange markets, said BA sales manager national accounts Warren Tempest. Other routes have not yet been affected but traffic to South Africa had made a slow start to 1997.

Against some currencies sterling is now standing some 25 percent up on a year ago and airlines are acutely aware that UK exports and rates can be seen as increasingly expensive in some overseas markets.

But the currency is not immediate with several months difference between placing of orders to and actual delivery. Also the invoicing currency will vary so the pattern will not be uniform, said Emirates UK cargo manager Ray Disson.
Also the cargo industry benefits from the boost in British that should result from a strong British pound, agents said.

Overall Disson said the market is looking pretty good - with rates unchanged since before Christmas - although business was quieter in the traditionally quiet January "but we get enough to comfortably fill flights."
"Business is going very nicely at 30 pct above on same period last year but this also reflects increased capacity provided by 777s," he added.
British Airways has attracted extra air cargo business this month on several routes with special promotional offers, industry and BA sources said.
"BA is actively promoting the North Atlantic routes with discounts but these are also available on other selected routes," BA national accounts sales manager Warren Tempest told Reuters.
On some routes these average upto 30 percent and require cargo to move within 48 hours of the offer being made, Tempest said adding that this is the normal notice BA receives from its customers.

The special offers which have been made across BA's world network including both directions over the N.Atlantic, from Europe and to and from southern Asia including India. Business has picked up from the first couple of weeks of January with the third week good to all Asian areas.
The Islamic month of Ramadan has helped reduced volume to the Middle East whilst traffic to the Far East will be hit by the start of the Chinese New Year.
"BA is only flying one rotation less for freighters to the Far East," Tempest said.
"Airlines should concentrate

Rates to Asia have been "a little bit soft" said Japan Air UK cargo manager Tony Edwards who is looking to a pick-up in business in February and March especially as ex-UK traffic should also be boosted by Japanese firms moving imports ahead of the end to the financial year in March.
Unusual cargoes for JAL include carrying 14 horses in February and 13 in March to Japan from the British racehorse sales held in Newmarket in November, he said.

Mark Boffee, UK/Ireland country manager of all-cargo airline Cargolux Airlines International said his UK-Singapore cargo business had recently been been good and he was optimistic about achieving further good yields over the next few months on the route.
"We have received regular enquiries about moving cargo from the UK to Hong Kong for at least the past two years, which we have had to turn down," Boffee said.
"But come July 1 and the end of cabotage on the route, we will introduce a new UK-Hong Kong cargo tariff. I am very optimistic about the future of this business for Cargolux."
Cargolux trucks all cargo from the UK to its Luxembourg hub where it loaded onto its fleet of 747-200/400 freighters.

The New Zealand economy and currency recovered faster from recession than the UK creating good demand from New Zealand consumers for foreign manufactured goods. Air New Zealand cargo sales manager for Europe Phil Rawlings said.
The recent rise in sterling had cut New Zealand imports from the UK, but if British goods are wanted to buy then Air NZ was often the preferred carrier for importers, he added.
"That is because we are now the only direct carrier on the London-Auckland route...that is where we have the edge over our competitors," he said.
On the North Atlantic, UK cargo manager for El Al Jacob Pianko said UK-Los Angeles traffic "is growing...our business in this market it getting stronger and stronger".

"From the UK, our main U.S. destination is New York and although we did not do too badly in the (pre-Christmas) peak season, for this market we were doing better in January 1996 than we are now," he said.
"But it is just the beginning of the year...it is too early to forecast any opinions on if and when the situation will improve. I don't want to make foolish predictions," he said.

El Al is a major cargo carrier from continental Europe to North America cargo carriers, operating between nine and 11 weekly 747 freighter services on the route. El Al feeds many of these flights from Britain by truck but also has space on its twice-weekly London Stansted (Heathrow in the summer)-New York 747 passenger flights.
El Al's UK-Chicago traffic was very strong in 1995 and this trend had continued into 1996, but recently had become much weaker. "Just why, I haven't a clue," said Pianko.

In contrast, Trans World Airlines' UK cargo sales and services manager Peter Simmonds said that Chicago would continue to be his and most other carriers' top U.S. cargo market in terms of yields during 1997.

"We had a good November and early December to Chicago but expected and got very little from December 26 to January 20 because the air cargo industry virtually closed down and then took 10 days to crank up again," he said.

"However, bookings are already picking up. Air cargo from the UK to Chicago is mainly heavy industrial goods -- engines, diesels, tractor parts and so on -- and I can see a small rate increase being introduced for this dense traffic in the spring. But not for lightweight goods because of the strong competition offered by the courier companies," said Simmonds.

In May TWA will be putting 20 tonnes capacity passenger Boeing 747-200/300s on its daily flights from London Gatwick to its St Louis hub instead of the current 767-200/300s, which can lift respectively eight and 15 tonnes.

At times TWA has attracted a lot of film, press and exhibition-related material from the UK to LA, but this business was not guaranteed on a regular basis as was the case with Chicago, Simmonds added.

"Los Angeles is an enigma market. But we are optimistic about achieving more success as the bigger, direct carriers on the route are tending to downsize their costly 747s in favour of twin-engine wide-bodies," he said.

"That means less cargo capacity available, leading some customers to switch to airlines like TWA which offer five to six Boeing 767 and Lockheed L-1011 connections a day from St Louis to the west coast. Unlike New York or Boston, traffic does not sit around for two to three days at St Louis -- same-day connections are met," Simmonds stated.
ANZ's Rawlings, agreed with TWA's description of the UK-U.S. west coast market, describing it as "unpredictable".

ANZ operates five weekly 747-400 passenger flights a week from London Heathrow and Frankfurt to Los Angeles, continuing on to Auckland. Capacity of 16 pallets or 35 tonnes of cargo a week is offered as far as LA.
"We fly mainly lightweight materials that are voluminous and take up a lot of space -- film production, pop group and publicity gear, not heavy machinery or parts," Rawlings said.

"The ex-UK market to LA is OK, but not all that buoyant. The problem is that there is so much competition on the route which adversely affects yields. Los Angeles is a tinseltown air cargo market and I can't see it improving," he added.
One bonus was that there is a large UK community living along the U.S. west coast which demands a good supply of UK manufactured goods, he said,
"But to offset that, there is all the competition in the marketplace," he added.

Rawlings said strong sterling had not had any significant affect on air cargo demand from California. "Our Los Angeles loads don't vary much on a month-to-month basis...they have been quite constant," he said.
Cargolux's Boffee said his ex-UK business to Los Angeles and San Francisco had been "good" in 1996,
"It continues to be steady and I am optimistic about achieving growth in the next few months," he added.
Boffee also said that Cargolux's ex-UK mainly general cargo loads, and yields, to Brazil had been quite busy over recent months and the state of the market in general was "fairly brisk".

Cargolux operates three weekly Luxembourg-Sao Paulo 747-400 services, which can each carry an average of 105 tonnes of cargo on the route. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
